title: Tests of whether Black bands could read
summary: Goodwin says doubters handed Black bands stock arrangements to test their reading.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well, I'll address this whole subject to Crook. What do you have to say about this?
Well, during this time you had people that were -- well you might say they were jazz buffs or whatever you might want to call them.

Well they were musicians and some people that were not musicians. They had an act that they would pull on especially a black band because it was a thing where it wasn't -- they weren't too sure that the black musicians could read and they would see a 12-piece band and

these -- well I would call them smart alecks -- they'd go and buy some charts, you know, just simple arrangements. We call them stocks, and they would bring them out on the band and they wanted to pass them around so all the guys, you know -- now this was just a test. It wasn't so much they wanted to hear the number because after they heard the number, it was probably some simple number that somebody -- nobody ever played, you know, but they wanted to have something that wasn't a number that was big on the charts but this number you wouldn't know.
Okay, this is a test, you know.
In other words, you couldn't play this from just having played it before. You had to be able to read it. (Simultaneous talk)
